caption: The sky field around the eclipsing binary NN Serpentis, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This is a working picture rather than a showpiece: a patch of sky around a faint star system called NN Serpentis, recorded through a visual filter in an exposure lasting only a few seconds. It was taken with the FORS1 instrument on ANTU, one of the unit telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope.

NN Serpentis is an eclipsing binary, a pair of stars whose orbit is lined up so that one periodically passes in front of the other, dimming the light we receive. ESO describes it as an unusual object, and astronomers planned to watch one of those eclipses as it happened.

Before they could, the telescope had to be pointed precisely. This frame was snapped just ahead of the eclipse observation, to centre the telescope on the right spot. It shows a slightly wider field than an earlier ESO press photo of the system and keeps the same orientation, so the two can be compared side by side.
explore: The system is very faint, listed at 17th magnitude, far too dim to see without a large telescope. It lies about 1600 light-years away, in the direction of Serpens Caput. In this frame, north lies about 20 degrees anticlockwise from the top.

understand.summary: The frame was taken with the FORS1 instrument on the VLT's ANTU telescope through a single visual (V) filter, so it records ordinary visible light in one band; no colour mapping is involved.
understand.eye: The object is far too faint for the unaided eye, and even this short telescope exposure gathers far more light than an eye could.

alt: A field of stars around the faint variable star system NN Serpentis, used to centre the telescope.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 362, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble resolves the individual stars of NGC 362, a globular cluster in our own galaxy. Globular clusters are dense, roughly spherical swarms holding hundreds of thousands of stars, and they tend to live in the outskirts of galaxies. The Milky Way has more than 150 of them, and this one stands out as unusual.

The reason lies in chemistry. Stars forge heavier elements in their cores as they age; astronomers lump everything heavier than hydrogen and helium together as metals. When stars die, they scatter that material into space, so each later generation starts out richer in metals than the one before.

When astronomers examined the elements in individual stars of NGC 362, they found a surprisingly high metal content. That points to a cluster younger than expected. Most globular clusters are far older than the bulk of their host galaxy's stars, but NGC 362's age falls between 10 and 11 billion years, while the Milky Way itself is estimated to be over 13 billion years old.
explore: The image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys. The cluster lies about 27,000 light-years from Earth.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys observed the cluster through blue, red and hydrogen-alpha filters in visible light. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's sharp view lets astronomers pick out the cluster's individual stars, which the eye could not separate.

alt: A dense globular cluster of countless individual stars seen by Hubble.

caption: The star cluster NGC 3590, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: Bright stars shine out in front of a dramatic backdrop: dark patches of dust and richly coloured clouds of glowing gas. The stars belong to NGC 3590, a small star cluster photographed at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile using the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope.

A star cluster like this is a family of stars born together from the same cloud of material. Because its members share a birthplace and roughly an age, the cluster works as a natural experiment, letting astronomers compare how stars of different masses develop over time. ESO notes that this modest gathering offers clues to how its stars formed and how they are changing.

It also has something to say about the bigger picture. The Milky Way is a spiral with arms that wind around its centre, and our place inside the disc makes their layout hard to map. Clusters such as NGC 3590 give astronomers hints about the structure of those pinwheeling arms.
explore: Besides the cluster itself, the frame takes in dark patches of dust and clouds of glowing gas. The picture was made with the Wide Field Imager camera, through blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha filters.

understand.summary: This image comes from the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope, using blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha filters in visible light. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, bringing out faint glowing gas and dust that would be invisible through a telescope eyepiece.

alt: Bright stars of a small cluster in front of dark dust patches and colourful glowing gas clouds.

caption: Wisps of the bubble Sh2-308 around EZ Canis Majoris, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A few fine threads of gas stretch across this Hubble view. They are part of Sh2-308, a faint, wispy shell in Canis Major, the Great Dog, some 5200 light-years away. The shell wraps around a single star, EZ Canis Majoris.

That star is a Wolf-Rayet star, a hugely bright type that is tens of times more massive than the Sun and sits at the extreme end of stellar evolution. The ancestors of such stars shed thick winds that stripped away their outer layers. The fierce, fast wind of the Wolf-Rayet star then sweeps up the surrounding material into bubbles.

EZ Canis Majoris cast off its own outer layers to make the strands seen here, and its intense radiation keeps pushing the bubble outward. Its edges are now about 60 light-years apart. Such bubbles do not last: the stars that inflate them will eventually explode as supernovae and swallow them.
explore: Wolf-Rayet stars rank with the most luminous and heaviest stars in the Universe. This frame shows only a few of the tenuous threads that make up the shell.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the gas through narrow filters that isolate light from oxygen and nitrogen. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The shell is described as faint and tenuous, far too dim for the eye; Hubble's narrow filters and long exposures pick out the glow of specific gases.

alt: Thin, wispy threads of glowing gas from a faint bubble around a massive star.

caption: The star cluster NGC 2100 and the Tarantula Nebula, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This wide view shows the dramatic neighbourhood of the star cluster NGC 2100, which lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small companion galaxy of the Milky Way. The cluster is only part of the story here: the frame is dominated by the Tarantula Nebula.

The Tarantula is the most active star-forming region in the Local Group, the collection of galaxies that includes the Milky Way. Star-forming regions are vast clouds of gas and dust where gravity pulls material together into new stars, and the young, hot stars that result light up the gas around them.

Putting NGC 2100 in context like this helps show how clusters and nebulae share the same galactic neighbourhood. The picture was assembled from visible-light exposures made with the Wide Field Imager, the camera mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope. Its wide field lets it take in the cluster and the sprawling nebula in a single frame.
explore: The region lies about 170,000 light-years away. The camera used blue, visual, oxygen and hydrogen-alpha filters, the last two picking out light from glowing gas.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope recorded this scene in visible light through blue, visual, oxygen and hydrogen-alpha filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The long exposures gather far more light than the eye, and the gas filters isolate the glow of particular elements.

alt: A wide field dominated by the Tarantula Nebula, which surrounds the star cluster NGC 2100.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 121, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's subject here is NGC 121, a globular cluster seen in the direction of Tucana, the Toucan. These clusters are big balls of old stars that circle the centres of their galaxies like satellites. This one belongs not to the Milky Way but to one of our neighbours, the Small Magellanic Cloud.

Because NGC 121 lies relatively close, Hubble can pick out its individual stars and study them in detail. Old clusters like this act as markers that trace the wider population of stars in the galaxy they belong to, helping astronomers learn how stars there formed and evolved.

NGC 121 is around 10 billion years old, the oldest cluster in its galaxy; the others there are 8 billion years old or younger. Yet it is still several billion years younger than comparable clusters in the Milky Way and the Large Magellanic Cloud. Why is not fully clear. Cluster formation may have been delayed in the Small Magellanic Cloud, or NGC 121 may be the lone survivor of an older group.
explore: English astronomer John Herschel discovered the cluster in 1835. The Milky Way has roughly 150 globular clusters. A version of this image was entered in the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition by Stefano Campani.

understand.summary: The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and Hubble's sharp vision resolves individual stars that an eye would see only as a hazy patch.

alt: A dense, rounded cluster of many individual stars.

caption: The star cluster Messier 18 and its surroundings, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Upper left of centre in this huge 615-megapixel ESO image sits a small smattering of bright blue stars. That little group is Messier 18, an open star cluster, and the rest of the frame takes in its surroundings.

An open cluster is a loose family of stars born together out of one massive cloud of gas and dust. Because its members share a birthplace and an age, differences between them come mainly down to mass. That makes Messier 18 an ideal laboratory for studying how stars live and die.

The picture was captured by OmegaCAM, the wide-field camera on the VLT Survey Telescope (VST) at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. The survey telescope is built to photograph large swathes of sky in fine detail, which is why this single image can take in such a broad field around the cluster.
explore: The camera recorded the scene through several visible and near-infrared filters, which were combined into the final colour picture.

understand.summary: OmegaCAM on the VLT Survey Telescope imaged the field through g, r and i visible filters and a near-infrared narrow-band filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared, which the eye cannot see, and the camera's exposures record many faint stars beyond the eye's reach.

alt: A wide field of stars with a small group of bright blue stars upper left of centre.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 92, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble captures Messier 92, a glittering globular cluster in the northern constellation of Hercules. A globular cluster is a ball of stars that orbits the core of a galaxy like a satellite, and this one is tightly packed with some 330 000 stars.

Among the Milky Way's globular clusters, Messier 92 ranks as one of the brightest, and under good conditions it can be seen with the naked eye. Like other globulars, it is made mostly of hydrogen and helium with only traces of anything else. It is classed as an Oosterhoff type II cluster, one of a family of clusters poor in metals, which is astronomers' term for every element beyond hydrogen and helium.

Studying the make-up of clusters like this helps astronomers work out their ages. Messier 92 turns out to be one of the oldest star clusters in our galaxy, with an age almost the same as that of the Universe.
explore: Astronomer Johann Elert Bode discovered the cluster in 1777. Gilles Chapdelaine submitted a version of this picture to the Hubble's Hidden Treasures image processing competition.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Messier 92 can be seen with the naked eye under good conditions, but the eye cannot separate its stars as Hubble does, and part of Hubble's data is near-infrared light the eye cannot see.

alt: A dense, bright ball of tightly packed stars.

caption: The core of the Hercules globular cluster Messier 13, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble gives an exceptionally clear look at the core of Messier 13, the great globular cluster in Hercules, where hundreds of thousands of stars crowd together. It is one of the brightest and best-known clusters in the sky, some 25,000 light-years away and about 145 light-years across.

Edmund Halley found it in 1714 and noted that, when the sky is clear and the Moon is absent, it is visible to the naked eye as a little patch. In 1974 the cluster was the target of a symbolic message sent from the Arecibo radio telescope, announcing humanity's existence to anyone who might be listening. More recent studies, though, suggest planets are very rare in the crowded environments of globular clusters.
Kurt Vonnegut wrote about the cluster in his 1959 novel The Sirens of Titan. The leap from Halley's early view to this Hubble portrait gives a sense of how far astronomy has come in three centuries.
explore: The image spans about 2.5 arcminutes of sky. Exposure times were 1480 seconds through the blue filter, 380 seconds through the red one and 567 seconds in near-infrared.

understand.summary: The image combines data from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a blue filter (F435W) shown in blue, a red filter (F625W) shown in green, and a near-infrared filter (F814W) shown in red.
understand.eye: Halley saw only a faint patch; Hubble's long exposures and near-infrared data, invisible to the eye, separate the core into individual stars.

alt: The densely packed core of a globular cluster, filled with countless stars.

caption: Part of the globular cluster NGC 6752, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble view shows part of NGC 6752, a globular cluster, one of the dense, ancient balls of stars that orbit our galaxy. At the top left, a collection of faint stars marks something that was not expected to be there at all: a galaxy far beyond the cluster.

Astronomers pointed Hubble at NGC 6752 to study its white dwarfs. A white dwarf is the small, dense remnant left behind when a Sun-like star uses up its fuel, and because white dwarfs cool at a predictable rate, they can be used as clocks to measure a cluster's age.

While analysing the data, the team spotted the previously unknown galaxy lying behind the cluster. It was nicknamed Bedin 1. The galaxy was an unexpected bonus: a study aimed at the cluster's own faint stars also turned up a far more distant neighbour hiding in the background.
explore: The discovery shows how a survey aimed at one target can reveal another. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and Bedin and colleagues.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the field through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Faint white dwarfs and the background galaxy are far too dim for the eye; Hubble's long exposures and near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, bring them out.

alt: Stars of a globular cluster, with a faint patch of stars marking a background galaxy at the top left.

caption: The Jewel Box cluster NGC 4755, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Several very bright, pale blue supergiant stars stand out in this close-up, along with a single ruby-red supergiant and a mix of other vividly coloured stars. Scattered among them are many much fainter stars, some with intriguing hues of their own. This is NGC 4755, better known as the Jewel Box cluster, seen by Hubble.

The Jewel Box is an open cluster, a group of stars that formed together and still travel as a family. Its members span a huge range of brightness because they span a wide range of mass: the brightest weigh in at 15 to 20 solar masses, whereas the faintest carry less than half the Sun's mass.

What makes this portrait special is its spread of light. It was the first image of an open galactic cluster to extend all the way from the far ultraviolet to the near-infrared, giving astronomers a view of these stars across a much wider range of wavelengths than the eye can see.
explore: The cluster lies about 6500 light-years away. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and is credited to NASA/ESA and Jesús Maíz Apellániz of the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Spain.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 observed the cluster through seven filters, from far-ultraviolet through visible to near-infrared. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are both invisible to the human eye, so much of the information in this picture lies outside what we could ever see directly.

alt: A star cluster with several bright pale blue stars, one ruby-red star and many fainter, variously coloured stars.

caption: Part of the Wild Duck Cluster, Messier 11, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars fill this Hubble view of part of Messier 11, an open cluster found in Scutum, the Shield, in the southern sky. It is nicknamed the Wild Duck Cluster because its brightest stars form a V shape a little like ducks flying in formation.

Messier 11 is among the richest and most compact open clusters known. By studying its brightest, hottest main-sequence stars, astronomers estimate its age at roughly 220 million years. Open clusters usually hold fewer and younger stars than globular clusters, and this one fits the pattern: at its centre are many blue stars, the hottest and youngest of its few thousand members.

Open clusters also do not last as long. Their stars are more widely spaced, so gravity holds them together less tightly, and stronger pulls from outside can drag them away. Messier 11 is likely to break up within a few million years as other objects nearby pull its stars off one at a time.
explore: Main-sequence stars are those in the long, steady middle of their lives, fusing hydrogen in their cores. Messier 11 lies about 6000 light-years away.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the cluster through an ultraviolet and a visible filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the human eye, which could never see this part of the data directly.

alt: A crowded field of stars from part of an open star cluster.

caption: The globular cluster Palomar 2, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This faint burst of stars is Palomar 2, a globular cluster captured by Hubble. Globular clusters are common and tend to look alike, but this one is unusual in several ways.

It belongs to a group of 15 globulars called the Palomar clusters, spotted on photographic plates taken in the 1950s for the first Palomar Observatory Sky Survey, whose team included Edwin Hubble. They were found so late because they are so faint: each is very remote, deeply hidden behind dust, or left with few stars.

Palomar 2 is the only globular cluster seen in its part of the sky, in Auriga, the Charioteer. Globulars orbit a galaxy's centre much as satellites circle Earth, so most lie closer to the galactic centre than we do and appear in the same general region of sky. Palomar 2 sits about five times farther out than other clusters, in the opposite direction, making it an outer-halo globular. A veil of dust also dims its stars.
explore: Hubble shows this cluster in a way smaller or ground-based telescopes could not. Some amateur astronomers with large telescopes take on the challenge of trying to spot all of the faint, well-hidden Palomar 15.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through a visible and a near-infrared filter. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Dust dims this cluster heavily; near-infrared light, invisible to the eye, passes through dust more easily than visible light.

alt: A faint scattering of stars forming a globular cluster, partly veiled by dust.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble looks into Messier 5, a globular cluster that is one of the oldest in the Milky Way. The bulk of its stars are more than 12 billion years old, but some surprising newcomers live among them.

Stars in a globular cluster are born together and age together. The most massive ones burn through their fuel in less than a million years and die as supernovae. That should have left Messier 5 with only old, low-mass stars, which cool into red giants, while the oldest move on to become blue horizontal branch stars.

Yet astronomers have found many young-looking blue stars hiding among the far brighter old ones. These latecomers are called blue stragglers, and astronomers think they formed either when stars collided or when one star in a close pair transferred mass to its partner. Both events are easy to imagine in a cluster where up to a few million stars are packed tightly together.
explore: Messier 5 lies about 25,000 light-years away in Serpens, the Snake. Exposure times were 750, 400 and 567 seconds through the blue, red and near-infrared filters, and the image spans about 2.6 arcminutes.

understand.summary: The picture comes from the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a blue filter (F435W) is shown in blue, a red filter (F625W) in green, and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the long exposures separate stars that would blend together for any eye at a telescope.

alt: A dense globular cluster packed with stars.

caption: The open cluster NGC 411, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: At first glance NGC 411 looks like a typical globular cluster, a crowd of stars of many colours and brightnesses. Appearances can deceive. It is not a globular cluster, its stars are not old, and it does not even belong to the Milky Way.

NGC 411 is classed as an open cluster. Such clusters are less tightly bound than globulars, and their stars drift apart over time, while globulars have endured for well over 10 billion years. NGC 411 is not much more than a tenth of that age, and its stars are only a fraction of the Sun's age.

All its stars formed at roughly the same time from a single cloud of gas, yet they come in different sizes. The range of colours and brightnesses in Hubble's view tells astronomers about each star's mass, temperature and stage of life. Blue stars, for example, have hotter surfaces than red ones.
explore: Around 150 globular clusters are scattered around our galaxy, and Hubble's sharp resolution picks out single stars even in their packed centres. NGC 411 lies about 200,000 light-years away.

understand.summary: This composite combines ultraviolet, visible and infrared observations from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3, reaching a little beyond both the violet and red ends of the spectrum. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The ultraviolet and infrared light in this image lie just beyond what the human eye can detect.

alt: A cluster of stars showing a wide range of colours and brightnesses.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6496, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble shows NGC 6496, a spherical globular cluster about 10.5 billion years old. Its stars are unusual: they hold much higher proportions of metals than stars in similar clusters. In astronomy, metals are all elements heavier than hydrogen and helium.

A handful of these metal-rich stars are variable stars, whose brightness changes over time. NGC 6496 hosts long-period variables, giant pulsating stars that can take a thousand days or more to change in brightness. It also has short-period eclipsing binaries, which dim when a companion star passes in front of them.

Watching how these stars vary can reveal their mass, radius, luminosity, temperature, composition and evolution. Those are measurements that would be hard or even impossible to obtain any other way, so variable stars are valuable tools for astronomers probing a cluster like this.
explore: Scottish astronomer James Dunlop discovered NGC 6496 in 1826. It lies in Scorpius, the Scorpion, a southern constellation, about 35,000 light-years from us. The image carries an acknowledgement to Judy Schmidt (Geckzilla).

understand.summary: The image combines data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3 through ultraviolet, blue, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, so part of this picture records light we could never see directly.

alt: A spherical globular cluster filled with many stars.

caption: The Dragon's Egg nebula NGC 6164/6165 around HD 148937, imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: A cloud of gas and dust surrounds a pair of stars in this image from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory. The nebula is NGC 6164/6165, also called the Dragon's Egg, and the stars at its heart are known together as HD 148937.

Astronomers using ESO data found that the two stars are surprisingly unlike each other. One appears much younger than the other, and only that one is magnetic. The nebula, too, is significantly younger than either star, and it is made of gases normally found deep inside a star rather than on its surface.

Put together, those clues pointed to a solution. The system most likely once held three stars, until two of them collided and merged into a single new, larger, magnetic star. That violent event is thought to have thrown out the material that now forms the nebula surrounding the surviving pair.
explore: The system lies about 4000 light-years away. The image is credited to the VPHAS+ survey team, with acknowledgement to CASU.

understand.summary: The image was taken in visible light with the VLT Survey Telescope. The source does not list the filters or publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: The long camera exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing faint nebula gas that would be very hard to see directly.

alt: A nebula of gas and dust surrounding a pair of stars.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6401, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's sharp optics break the globular cluster NGC 6401 into its individual stars. Through older telescopes it looked like a ghostly mist. The cluster lies in Ophiuchus, the Serpent Bearer, and is faint enough that seeing it takes a telescope and some experience.

Globular clusters are rich, generally spherical groups of stars that orbit the cores of galaxies, bound together by gravity. The Milky Way has around 160, and they contain some of the oldest stars known. Their origin and role in how galaxies evolve are still not fully understood.

NGC 6401 has fooled observers before. William Herschel discovered it in 1784 but thought it was a bright nebula, and his son John made the same mistake. In 1977 astronomers thought they had found a planetary nebula in it, but a 1990 study concluded the object is a symbiotic star: a red giant paired with a small hot star, wrapped in nebulosity.
explore: Because symbiotic stars are thought to turn into a kind of planetary nebula in time, the 1977 claim may simply have been early. Exposure times were 680 and 580 seconds, and the field of view is 3.3 by 1.5 arcminutes.

understand.summary: This image uses the Wide Field Channel of Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys: a yellow-orange filter (F606W) is shown in blue and a near-infrared filter (F814W) in red.
understand.eye: Where early observers saw a misty patch, Hubble resolves separate stars, and part of the data is near-infrared light invisible to the eye.

alt: A globular cluster resolved into many individual stars.

caption: The central parts of Omega Centauri, imaged by the TRAPPIST telescope at La Silla
story: This image shows the central parts of Omega Centauri, a globular cluster that contains as many as ten million stars. It was among the objects observed at first light by TRAPPIST, a national telescope at La Silla. First light is the moment a new telescope makes its first observations.
The picture spans 20 arcminutes of sky yet covers only the cluster's central parts. It combines data taken through three filters, labelled B, V and R.

TRAPPIST, short for TRAnsiting Planets and PlanetesImals Small Telescope, was built to study planetary systems in two ways. One is to detect and characterise exoplanets, planets orbiting stars other than the Sun. The other is to study comets orbiting the Sun. The 60-centimetre telescope is operated remotely from Liège, in Belgium, 12 000 km away.
explore: Omega Centauri lies about 17,000 light-years away. The image is credited to TRAPPIST, E. Jehin and ESO.

understand.summary: TRAPPIST imaged the cluster in visible light through blue (B), visual (V) and red (R) filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The camera exposures gather far more light than the eye, resolving many stars in the cluster's centre.

alt: The central region of a large globular cluster of stars.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 62, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Most globular clusters are nearly perfect spheres of stars, but Messier 62 is distorted. The 12-billion-year-old cluster stretches out on one side into a comet-like shape, with a bright head and an extended tail. It is one of the closest globulars to our galaxy's centre, and strong tidal forces there likely pull many of its stars out of place.

Globular clusters tend to be denser towards their centres, and the more massive a cluster, the denser that centre is likely to be. Weighing almost a million Suns, Messier 62 ranks among the densest globulars. Stars there interact and merge regularly, and huge stars burn out fast, explode, and leave behind white dwarfs, neutron stars and, sometimes, black holes.
For years, astronomers believed black holes would soon be kicked out of globular clusters. In 2013, though, one was found in Messier 62, the first in a Milky Way globular cluster.
explore: That discovery opened a new hunting ground for black holes. Messier 62 lies about 22,000 light-years away.

understand.summary: This view combines ultraviolet and visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet light is invisible to the human eye, and Hubble resolves stars in the cluster's dense core that an eye could not separate.

alt: A dense star cluster stretched on one side into a comet-like shape with a bright head and a tail.

caption: The globular cluster Ruprecht 106, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble acts like a giant detective's magnifying glass in this star-filled view of Ruprecht 106, a globular cluster that poses a puzzle. The stars in a globular cluster all formed at roughly the same place and time.

Even so, nearly every globular cluster turns out to hold groups of stars with distinct chemical make-ups. These fingerprints come from populations whose ages or compositions differ very slightly from the rest of the cluster. Only a tiny handful of globulars lack these multiple populations, and Ruprecht 106 is one of that small, mysterious group, which is why astronomers are looking at it closely.

The picture was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys, one of Hubble's most versatile instruments. Hubble's instruments have generations of their own: this camera is a third-generation instrument that replaced the original Faint Object Camera in 2002. Similarly, Wide Field Camera 3 replaced WFPC2, which had itself replaced the camera installed at launch.
explore: Space Shuttle astronauts serviced Hubble in orbit five times, upgrading ageing equipment and swapping in newer, more capable instruments. That work has kept the telescope at the forefront of astronomy for more than three decades. The image is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and A. Dotter.

understand.summary: The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys through visible (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: One of Hubble's filters records near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: A globular cluster studded with many individual stars.

caption: The star cluster Terzan 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows Terzan 5, a stellar cluster hidden in the bulge, the dense, dusty crowd of stars around the centre of the Milky Way. Thick dust clouds lie between us and the cluster, so seeing its stars clearly means peering through that veil.
An international team of astronomers did just that and found an unusual mix of stars in the cluster. Their observations showed that the stars in Terzan 5 are a surprisingly varied population.

The results suggest that Terzan 5 is really one of the bulge's primordial building blocks. In other words, it is most likely a relic from the very early days of the Milky Way, a surviving fragment of the material from which the central part of our galaxy was assembled. Studying it offers a way to look back at how our galaxy came together.
explore: The image combines Hubble data from the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3, and the release credits ESO and F. Ferraro.

understand.summary: The image combines visible and near-infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and near-infrared data from Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and it passes through dust more easily than visible light, which helps reveal stars behind the bulge's thick dust clouds.

alt: A dense field of stars in a cluster seen through the dusty central region of the Milky Way.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 4833, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble shows NGC 4833, a tightly packed swarm of stars in the constellation of Musca, the Fly, approximately 22,000 light-years away. It is a globular cluster, a dense, roughly spherical gathering of stars.

NGC 4833 is one of more than 150 globular clusters known in the Milky Way. These clusters are thought to hold some of the oldest stars in our galaxy, which makes them useful to astronomers. By studying them, researchers can piece together how a galaxy formed and changed over time, and estimate how old it is.

Globular clusters are among the most striking sights in the sky, with hundreds of thousands of stars gathered in one region of space. Hubble has photographed many of them from its orbit around Earth, and each of those views shows a dense gathering of stars in fine detail.
explore: Because these clusters are thought to hold some of our galaxy's oldest stars, they can also give an idea of the galaxy's age. This image was made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6441, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The stars of NGC 6441 glitter like snowflakes in this Hubble view. This globular cluster sits about 13,000 light-years from the centre of the Milky Way. As with snowflakes, the exact number of stars is hard to pin down.

Together, its stars are estimated to weigh 1.6 million times as much as the Sun. By that measure, NGC 6441 counts among the heaviest and brightest of our galaxy's globular clusters. It hosts four pulsars, spinning stellar remnants that each complete a rotation in a few milliseconds.

Also hidden in the cluster is JaFu 2, a planetary nebula. Despite the name, planetary nebulae have little to do with planets. They are a stage in the lives of intermediate-mass stars, lasting only a few tens of thousands of years, a mere moment on astronomical timescales, so each one is a short-lived phase in a star's life.
explore: The Milky Way has about 150 known globular clusters. They contain some of the first stars a galaxy produces, yet exactly how they formed and evolved remains unclear to astronomers.

caption: Stars in the crowded central bulge of the Milky Way, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A crowd of stars fills this Hubble view of the heart of our galaxy. Ageing red giants mingle with their more plentiful younger relatives, smaller, white, Sun-like stars, in the Milky Way's ancient central hub, known as the bulge. Most of the bright blue stars are probably recently formed stars in the foreground, in the galaxy's disc.

Working through nine years of archived Hubble images, astronomers tracked 10 000 of these Sun-like stars, looking for clues to how our galaxy evolved. They found the bulge is a busy place, where stars of different ages move at different speeds, like travellers rushing through an airport.

How a star moves depends on its chemistry. Stars with more elements beyond hydrogen and helium move in a more orderly way, yet they circle the galactic centre faster than older stars that lack such elements.
explore: The data were gathered for the Galactic Bulge Treasury Program and for the Sagittarius Window Eclipsing Extrasolar Planet Search, two separate Hubble surveys. Our galaxy's centre lies roughly 26 000 light-years from Earth.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 2108, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A gleaming ruby-red spot sits at the centre left of this colourful globular cluster, like a watchful eye. The cluster is NGC 2108, which sits inside the Large Magellanic Cloud, in the direction of Dorado, the Swordfish.

That red eye is in fact a carbon star, a type of star that is nearly always a cool red giant with an atmosphere containing more carbon than oxygen, the reverse of the Sun. In the star's outer layer, carbon and oxygen join up as carbon monoxide until the oxygen runs out.

The leftover carbon is then free to build other compounds, including molecules such as C2, CH and CN. These molecules scatter blue light inside the star while letting red light pass through, which is why the star glows such a deep red among its neighbours. That chemistry is what lets a single star stand out so clearly within the cluster.
explore: John Herschel, astronomer, mathematician, chemist and inventor, and son of William Herschel, discovered the cluster in 1835. It lies about 150,000 light-years away.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys captured the cluster through three filters, blue, visual and near-infrared. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.

caption: The star cluster Westerlund 2, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This is the sparkling centrepiece of Hubble's 25th anniversary tribute: Westerlund 2, a giant cluster of about 3000 stars. It lies 20,000 light-years away in the constellation Carina.

Westerlund 2 sits inside a stellar nursery, a region where new stars are forming from clouds of gas and dust. That dust normally hides much of what lies within, because it blocks and scatters visible light.

Hubble's near-infrared camera gets around the problem. Infrared light passes through dust far more easily, so the telescope can see through the dusty veil around the nursery. The result is a sharp look at the tightly packed stars at the heart of the cluster, a crowd that would otherwise be largely obscured. It shows how the choice of wavelength can turn a murky cloud into a detailed portrait of the stars inside it.
explore: The image draws on two of Hubble's cameras, the Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. It is credited to NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team, A. Nota and the Westerlund 2 Science Team.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 2, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble turns its gaze on Messier 2, a globular cluster some 55,000 light-years away in Aquarius, the Water-Bearer. A globular cluster is a spherical group of stars held tightly together by gravity.
Messier 2 is roughly 175 light-years across and home to 150 000 stars. At about 13 billion years old, it ranks among the largest clusters of its type and one of the oldest linked to the Milky Way.

Most of its mass is concentrated at the centre, and shimmering streams of stars extend outward from that dense core. It is bright enough to be seen with the naked eye when conditions are extremely good. Hubble's view reveals the stars that make it up. Star clusters like this are favourite subjects for cosmic photoshoots, and Hubble's keen eye is often turned on them.
explore: At around 13 billion years old, Messier 2 is among the oldest clusters associated with the Milky Way. The image comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and G. Piotto and colleagues.

caption: The star cluster and nebula NGC 371, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This picture shows the star cluster NGC 371 and the nebula that surrounds it. The FORS1 instrument captured it from ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, where it was mounted on the Very Large Telescope.

NGC 371 is not in the Milky Way. Its home is the Small Magellanic Cloud, a close galactic neighbour. Studying clusters in a neighbouring galaxy lets astronomers compare star formation there with what happens at home.

A star cluster wrapped in a nebula is typically a place where stars have formed out of the surrounding clouds of gas. Young, hot stars give off energetic light that makes nearby gas glow. The filters used for this image isolate light from helium and hydrogen, the kinds of emission such glowing gas produces. Here that means a cluster and its surrounding nebula, seen in a galaxy beyond our own.
explore: The Small Magellanic Cloud region lies about 200,000 light-years away. The image is credited to ESO and Manu Mejias.

caption: The super star cluster Westerlund 1, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble looks at Westerlund 1, a young super star cluster about 15,000 light-years away. That may sound enormous, but on a cosmic scale it is close: an object at that distance still lies within our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

Among its members is one of the largest stars ever found, first named Westerlund 1-26. Astronomers identified it while classifying the cluster's stars by spectral type, temperature and brightness. It is a red supergiant, sometimes classed as a hypergiant, with a radius more than 1500 times the Sun's. Placed where the Sun is, it would reach beyond the orbit of Jupiter.

Most of the cluster's stars are thought to have formed in a single burst, so they share similar ages and compositions. At around three million years old, the cluster is a baby next to the Sun, whose age is some 4.6 billion years.
explore: Light moves at just under 300 000 kilometres per second. A light-year, despite the name, is a distance: how far light travels in a year, around nine trillion kilometres.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the cluster in near-infrared light through three filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.

caption: The superbubble LHA 120-N 44 around the star cluster NGC 1929, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: This view from ESO's Very Large Telescope shows the nebula LHA 120-N 44, which surrounds the star cluster NGC 1929. The region lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy that orbits our own Milky Way.

N 44 is a place where stars are being born, and its most striking feature is a colossal superbubble: a vast cavity of material that is expanding outward. The driving force is the cluster of young stars at the bubble's heart. Massive young stars pour out intense radiation and powerful winds, and many end their lives in supernova explosions, all of which can push surrounding gas outward.

In this way the cluster sculpts the interstellar landscape around it and pushes the nebula's evolution forward. The same stars that formed from the cloud end up reshaping it. Regions like this let astronomers watch that cycle of creation and reshaping in a neighbouring galaxy.
explore: The region lies about 170,000 light-years away. The image was taken with the FORS1 instrument through filters that pick out light from helium, oxygen and hydrogen. It is credited to ESO and Manu Mejias.

understand.summary: FORS1 on the Very Large Telescope imaged the nebula through narrow filters isolating ionised helium, doubly ionised oxygen, neutral helium and hydrogen-alpha light. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the telescope's exposures reveal faint structure in another galaxy that the eye could not see.

caption: The double star cluster NGC 1850, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Threads of filamentary nebulosity surround this young star cluster, NGC 1850, seen by Hubble. The filamentary pattern is thought to have been created by supernova blasts. The cluster lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, one of the dwarf galaxies that neighbour the Milky Way.

NGC 1850 is a double cluster. At the centre is a main cluster that resembles a globular cluster, though it is young. Below and to the right sits a second, younger and smaller cluster. That companion contains extremely hot blue stars alongside fainter red T Tauri stars, which are very young stars that have not yet settled into steady hydrogen burning.

Having such a wide variety of stars in one place is a gift to astronomers. It allows a thorough study of how stars form, from massive, brilliant stars to modest newborns still in the earliest stage of their lives, all close together in the same patch of sky.
explore: NGC 1850 lies about 180,000 light-years away. The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and credits ESA, NASA and Martino Romaniello of the European Southern Observatory.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the cluster through blue, visual, red, near-infrared and hydrogen-alpha filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's long exposures reveal faint filaments of gas and individual stars in another galaxy that no eye could make out.

caption: The Herbig-Haro objects HH 46 and HH 47, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thin, spindly jets of matter stretch across this Hubble image, drifting among surrounding gas and stars. These are HH 46 and HH 47, two Herbig-Haro objects in the constellation of Vela, the Sails, more than 1400 light-years from Earth. Herbig-Haro objects are among the rarer sights in the night sky.

For years, how such multicoloured objects formed was a mystery. Before 1997, R. D. Schwartz, who discovered this pair in 1977, and others suggested they might be a kind of reflection nebula, or shock waves made where gas from a star meets surrounding matter.

The answer came with the discovery of a protostar, a star still forming, at the centre of the long jets, though it is not visible here. The newborn star flung out the outflows, which span some 10 light-years, at more than 150 kilometres per second. Where they slammed into surrounding gas, bright shock waves formed.
explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 using filters that isolate light from oxygen, iron and hydrogen. It is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and B. Nisini.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the jets in visible and near-infrared light, including filters tuned to oxygen, ionised iron and hydrogen (Paschen beta) emission. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Several of the filters record near-infrared light, which is invisible to the eye, so much of this picture shows light we could never see directly.

caption: The galaxy merger Arp 220, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: A brilliant six-pointed orange light dominates this Webb view, wrapped in wisps of orange gas and bluish-purple haze, with many other galaxies around it. It looks like a star, but it is Arp 220: two spiral galaxies in the middle of merging, their cores coming together.

Arp 220 shines brightest in infrared light, which makes it an ideal Webb target. It is an ultra-luminous infrared galaxy, glowing with more than a trillion suns' worth of light, against the Milky Way's roughly ten billion. The collision began about 700 million years ago and set off an enormous burst of star formation. Around 200 huge star clusters crowd a dusty region about 5000 light-years across.

Hubble earlier found the two parent cores 1200 light-years apart. Each has a rotating ring of star formation blazing in infrared, and that glare produces the diffraction spikes. On the outskirts, Webb shows faint tidal tails in blue, and organic material appears in reddish-orange streams.
explore: Arp 220 lies 250 million light-years away in Serpens and is the 220th entry in Halton Arp's Atlas of Peculiar Galaxies. It is the nearest such galaxy and the brightest of the three mergers closest to Earth. Radio telescopes found about 100 supernova remnants in an area under 500 light-years across.

understand.summary: Webb's NIRCam and MIRI observed Arp 220 in near- and mid-infrared light. Shorter wavelengths (0.9 and 1.5 microns) are shown in blue, 2.0 microns in green, 2.77 and 7.7 microns in yellow, 3.56 microns in orange, and 4.44 and 11 microns in red.
understand.eye: Webb's infrared light is invisible to the eye, so the colours here are a translation, with shorter infrared wavelengths shown bluer and longer ones redder.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6558, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars in a rich variety of hues throng this Hubble image of NGC 6558, a globular cluster. Some of the brightest carry prominent diffraction spikes, imaging artefacts made when starlight interacts with the structure inside the telescope.

NGC 6558 lies about 23 000 light years away in Sagittarius, nearer our galaxy's centre than we are. Globular clusters are tightly bound collections of anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars, found in many kinds of galaxies, and as this view shows, their stars can be packed very densely.

They also serve as natural laboratories. A globular cluster's stars were born at roughly one time with a similar starting composition, so astronomers can compare how various stars develop when starting conditions match. The picture belongs to a set of observations of globular clusters in the inner Milky Way, aimed at understanding how those clusters form and change.
explore: The image was captured with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and R. Cohen.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged the cluster through visible (F606W) and near-infrared (F814W) filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Near-infrared light is invisible to the eye, and the spikes around bright stars are an artefact of the telescope, not something in the sky.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6355, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars cover this Hubble view from edge to edge. Towards the centre they crowd into an even denser circular region that also looks bluer, while redder foreground stars sit around the edges and many small stars fill the background. This is NGC 6355, a globular cluster less than 50,000 light-years away in Ophiuchus.

NGC 6355 lives in the inner regions of the Milky Way. Globular clusters are stable, tightly bound groups of tens of thousands to millions of stars. Their crowding and mutual gravity give them a roughly round shape: a bright core fading into an ever sparser sprinkling of stars. Hubble captured this cluster's dense core in sharp detail.

From above the blurring of Earth's atmosphere, Hubble has transformed the study of globular clusters. From the ground, telling their stars apart is almost impossible, but Hubble lets astronomers examine them one by one.
explore: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 and Advanced Camera for Surveys both contributed data to this picture, which is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA, E. Noyola and R. Cohen.

understand.summary: The image combines blue, visible and near-infrared data from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys and Wide Field Camera 3. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Hubble's position above the atmosphere lets it separate stars that would blur together for any eye or ground telescope, and one filter records near-infrared light we cannot see.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 5, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This sparkling jumble of stars is Messier 5, a globular cluster of hundreds of thousands of stars held together by their shared gravity. ESA/Hubble likens the scene to cosmic fairy lights.

Messier 5 is not an ordinary globular cluster. At 13 billion years old, it dates back almost to the Universe's own beginning, some 13.8 billion years ago. It ranks among the largest clusters known, and lying only 24 500 light-years from us, it is a favourite target for astronomers' telescopes.

It also holds a puzzle. Stars in a globular cluster grow old together, so by now Messier 5 should contain old, low-mass red giants and other ancient stars. Instead it is teeming with young-looking blue stars called blue stragglers. These unexpected stars come to life when stars collide, or when one star strips material from another.
explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 using ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 imaged the cluster through ultraviolet, visible, hydrogen-alpha and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Ultraviolet and near-infrared light are invisible to the eye, and Hubble resolves individual stars that would blend together for an eye at a telescope.

caption: The globular cluster Liller 1, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: The muted red glow of the globular cluster Liller 1 is partly hidden here behind a dense scattering of piercing blue stars. Liller 1 lies a fairly neighbourly 30,000 light-years away, but it sits inside the Milky Way's bulge, the dense, dusty region at the galaxy's centre.

That dust scatters visible light, especially blue light, very effectively, so the cluster is heavily obscured. Some red and infrared light gets through, though. According to ESA/Hubble, the camera used here is sensitive to both visible and near-infrared light, which lets it see through the dust clouds to the cluster.

Liller 1 is unusual because it contains both very old and very young stars, whereas globular clusters usually contain only old stars. Liller 1 has at least two distinct populations: the oldest is 12 billion years old, and the youngest just 1 to 2 billion years old. Astronomers concluded it was able to form stars over an extraordinarily long time.
explore: Near-infrared light lies just beyond the red end of the visible spectrum. The image is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and F. Ferraro.

caption: The dusty ring around the double star IRAS 08544-4431, imaged by the Very Large Telescope Interferometer
story: This is not a conventional photograph but a reconstructed image from the Very Large Telescope Interferometer at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. It shows the dusty disc around IRAS 08544-4431, a close pair of ageing stars, and according to ESO it is the sharpest view ever obtained of such a disc.

An interferometer combines light from several telescopes to see much finer detail than any one of them could manage alone. In this view the brighter central star has been removed. A fainter glow from the second star remains visible, which surprised the observers.

For the first time, discs like this one around old stars can be compared with the discs that surround young stars, and they look surprisingly alike. Young stars' discs are where planets are born. That raises an intriguing possibility: a disc that forms near the end of a star's life might also build a second generation of planets.
explore: The system lies about 4000 light-years away. The observations were made in near-infrared light with the PIONIER instrument.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1559 and supernova SN 2005df, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: The spiral galaxy NGC 1559 is the subject of this colour image, and just above it shines a bright point of light that is not an ordinary star. It is a supernova, SN 2005df, the explosion of a star inside the galaxy. The picture was made with the FORS1 instrument on ESO's 8.2-metre Very Large Telescope.

A supernova can briefly outshine huge numbers of ordinary stars, which is why a single dying star can appear so bright beside an entire galaxy. Astronomers watch these explosions closely to learn how stars end their lives.

NGC 1559 lies in the constellation Reticulum, the Reticle. Beyond it, the image also captures many background galaxies, far more distant islands of stars scattered across the field. The combination makes this a snapshot of a galaxy at a particular moment, marked by a single stellar explosion.
explore: NGC 1559 lies about 50 million light-years away. Note that the release title names the supernova SN 2005dh, while its caption calls it SN 2005df.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 1806, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble's sharp view turns NGC 1806 into a sparkling ball of tens of thousands of stars, all bound together by gravity. Clusters like this are called globular clusters, and most are very old, having formed long ago, when the cosmos was far younger than it is now.

NGC 1806 is not in our galaxy. It lies in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite of the Milky Way, and appears in the constellation of Dorado, the dolphin-fish, which is best seen from Earth's southern hemisphere.

The British astronomer John Herschel discovered it in 1836. He had travelled to South Africa to catalogue objects best seen from southern latitudes, completing work begun by his father, William, who coined the term globular cluster. That same year, Charles Darwin visited him when HMS Beagle stopped at Cape Town, and Darwin later called Herschel one of "our greatest philosophers". Herschel also contributed to photography, so this picture would surely have delighted him.
explore: Exposure times were 770, 720 and 688 seconds, and the frame covers 3.1 by 1.9 arcminutes of sky. John Herschel scanned the sky with a large telescope and noted objects of interest, NGC 1806 among them.

caption: The protoplanetary disc Oph 163131, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope, Hubble and ALMA
story: Two flat purple lobes meet in the middle of this image, with yellow rings along the midplane. The whole disc glows, sending bands of green, blue and red light into the dark around it, while white stars and distant orange galaxies dot the background. This is Oph 163131, a protoplanetary disc about 480 light-years away in Ophiuchus.

At its centre is a newborn star still wrapped in gas and dust. Before the star's radiation clears the dust away, grains may clump into pebbles, planetesimals and eventually planets. The disc is nearly edge-on and some 66 billion kilometres wide, several times the span of our Solar System, so it suits close study well.

The yellow disc is made of larger, millimetre-sized grains seen by ALMA, concentrated in the central plane. It shows two rings separated by a gap, possibly where a planet is forming and clearing dust. Small grains above and below scatter starlight, producing the purple arcs.
explore: An edge-on view shows whether large grains are settling into a layer at the disc's core, which is critical for planet growth; the thicker, the better. The disc may even hold a clump of gas on its way to becoming a planet. The glow around the disc is brightest in MIRI's mid-infrared data.

understand.summary: The picture merges Hubble visible light (shown in blue), Webb NIRCam near-infrared at 2.0 and 4.44 microns (cyan and green), Webb MIRI mid-infrared at 7.7, 12 and 21 microns (yellow, orange and red) and ALMA millimetre-wave data (orange).

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6139, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This rich, dense smattering of stars is NGC 6139, a massive globular cluster that orbits the Milky Way, held together by its own gravity. It is seen roughly in the direction of our galaxy's centre, in the constellation of Scorpius, the Scorpion.

Globular clusters are denser and rounder than open clusters such as the well-known Pleiades. They usually hold hundreds of thousands of stars thought to have formed at about the same time. Studies show that NGC 6139 is home to an ageing population. Most globular clusters around the Milky Way are estimated to be more than 10 billion years old, so they contain some of our galaxy's oldest stars, formed very early in its history.
Even so, exactly what role these clusters played in how galaxies evolve is still being studied. Scorpius, a constellation full of fascinating objects, is a place Hubble has looked many times.
explore: Among Hubble's other targets in Scorpius are the butterfly-shaped Bug Nebula, surprising binary star systems and other globular clusters. NGC 6139 lies about 35,000 light-years away.

caption: The Necklace Nebula, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A glowing ring studded with bright clumps of gas circles a single bright dot in this Hubble image, like a necklace of diamonds. This is the Necklace Nebula, a planetary nebula 15,000 light-years away in the small, faint constellation of Sagitta, the Arrow.

It was made by two Sun-like stars locked in a tight orbit. Roughly 25 000 years ago, one of them swelled up and swallowed its smaller companion, forming what astronomers call a common envelope. The smaller star kept orbiting inside the bloated giant, spinning it faster until large parts of it were flung into space. That escaping debris became the ring, with dense clumps forming the bright diamonds.
The two stars remain so close, only a few million kilometres apart, that they appear as one bright dot at the centre. They still race around one another, each lap taking just over a day.
explore: The nebula's catalogue name is PN G054.2-03.4. Hubble had featured it before, but advanced processing techniques gave this new, improved view. In March 2024 ESA corrected the age of the event to 25 000 years from an earlier figure.

understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, a separation the eye cannot make.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Thousands of bright points of light fill this Hubble view, gathered a little more thickly towards the centre. Their colours vary, and the most prominent ones look blue or yellow-orange, and the brighter ones show four diffraction spikes, an effect of the telescope's structure. This is Messier 4, a globular cluster.

A globular cluster is a dense, roughly spherical swarm of stars bound together by gravity, and Messier 4 holds several hundred thousand of them. The colours of the stars carry information: in general, hotter stars look bluer and cooler stars look redder.

Messier 4 may also hide something in its core. Astronomers suspect an unseen intermediate-mass black hole of up to 800 solar masses sits there. Such black holes would sit between the small ones left by single stars and the giants at galaxy centres, but whether one really exists here is not yet confirmed.
explore: Messier 4 lies about 7000 light-years away. The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

caption: A star field in Sagittarius, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Across this Hubble frame lie scattered stars of deep red and bright blue, set against thousands of more distant stars and galaxies. The scene is a slice of sky in the constellation of Sagittarius, the Archer. Two features catch the eye: the colours of the stars, and the crosses bursting from the brightest ones.

Some colours were enhanced when the image was processed, but stars really do shine in different colours. Colour depends on surface temperature: very hot stars look blue or white, cooler ones redder. A star may be cooler because it is small, or because it is old and has become a red giant, swelling and cooling as its core collapses.

The crosses are diffraction spikes. They come neither from the stars nor from the atmosphere, since Hubble orbits above it. Struts holding Hubble's secondary mirror, arranged in a cross, slightly bend incoming light around their edges. Each cross in this frame comes from that single set of struts.
explore: Those supporting struts are known as telescope spiders. Although the spikes are technically an imperfection, many astrophotographers choose to highlight them as an attractive part of their pictures.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 1466, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble reveals NGC 1466, an ancient, glimmering ball of stars. It is a globular cluster, a group of stars held together by gravity, moving slowly along the fringes of the Large Magellanic Cloud, a nearby neighbour galaxy.

NGC 1466 is a cluster of extremes. It holds a mass equal to roughly 140 000 Suns and is around 13.1 billion years old, almost as old as the Universe itself. That makes it something like a fossil left over from the early cosmos, preserving stars that formed very long ago.

Astronomers are interested in more than its age. NGC 1466 is one of five clusters in the Large Magellanic Cloud whose level of dynamical evolution has been measured. This so-called dynamical age describes how far the cluster's internal structure has changed as its stars interact gravitationally over time, which is different from simply how old its stars are.
explore: The caption places the cluster some 160 000 light-years away, while catalogue data lists about 150,000 light-years.

caption: The star cluster NGC 2203, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble presents the star cluster NGC 2203 in the sharpest view yet obtained of it. Beyond its good looks, the cluster holds plenty of treats that have helped astronomers piece together how stars live.

Most of a star's life is spent on what astronomers call the main sequence, the long, steady stage when it burns fuel at an even pace. The Sun is a main-sequence star. In approximately 6 billion years its fuel will run out, and it will move on to its next stage and become a red giant.

NGC 2203 contains stars roughly twice as massive as the Sun. Astronomers studying them found that rotation might help explain why some of these stars linger longer than usual in the main-sequence phase. How fast a star spins, in other words, may affect how long it stays in this long, steady stage of its life.
explore: The image was made with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 through ultraviolet, blue-green and near-infrared filters, and is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and L. Girardi.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6540, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars pack this Hubble view of NGC 6540, a globular cluster in Sagittarius. The brightest wear prominent cross-shaped diffraction spikes. These are imaging artefacts: as starlight passes into the telescope, the hardware inside nudges it slightly, so bright objects gain spikes of light.

A globular cluster is a stable, tightly bound group of stars, from tens of thousands to millions, held close by their mutual gravity. The image combines two Hubble cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys. Their fields of view differ slightly, so the picture shows only the patch of sky both captured.

Hubble looked into the cluster's heart as part of an effort to gauge how old, how shaped and how structured the globular clusters near our galaxy's centre are. Gas and dust there block some of their light and subtly change the colours of their stars. Because these clusters hold clues to our galaxy's earliest history, studying them helps trace how it evolved.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 265, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A myriad of stars appears in crisp detail in this Hubble image of NGC 265, which ESA/Hubble describes as the most detailed image of the cluster to date. It was taken with the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

NGC 265 is an open star cluster, a loose group of stars that formed together from the same cloud of gas and dust. Unlike the dense, ancient globular clusters, open clusters are usually younger and more spread out, and over time their members drift apart.

This one lies in the Small Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way, about 200,000 light-years away. It measures roughly 65 light-years across. At such a distance, separating the stars of a cluster from one another is a challenge, and Hubble's sharp vision is what makes a view this clear possible. Studying clusters in a neighbouring galaxy lets astronomers compare how stars form there with how they form in our own.

caption: A field of stars and galaxies beside the cluster NGC 299, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hundreds of distant stars and galaxies fill this Hubble frame, yet the object Hubble was actually studying is nowhere to be seen. The Advanced Camera for Surveys has two detectors. One recorded the real target, an open star cluster called NGC 299, while the other photographed the patch of sky just next to it. This is that second view.

It is technically a sidekick picture, but it is full of interest. Many of the tiny objects that look like stars are really galaxies. The spirals show arms curving out from bright centres, while fuzzier, less defined shapes may be elliptical galaxies. Some hold millions upon millions of stars, yet are so far away that all of them fit into a pinprick no bigger than a single star.

Blue points mark very hot stars, a few stretched into crosses by the struts that hold Hubble's secondary mirror. Red points mark cooler stars, perhaps red giants, dying stars that have cooled and swollen.
explore: The Advanced Camera for Surveys is a highly efficient wide-field camera that covers both visible and near-infrared light.

caption: The Tau Canis Majoris Cluster, NGC 2362, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: One star dominates the centre of this ESO picture: Tau Canis Majoris, a massive multiple star system that outshines every other member of its home cluster, NGC 2362, in Canis Major, the Great Dog. Around it are many fainter young stars, only four or five million years old and just starting their lives.

NGC 2362, often named after that bright star, is an open cluster whose stars all emerged from one molecular cloud. Its members share a chemical make-up and are loosely held together by gravity. Having been born together, they form an ideal laboratory for testing ideas about stellar evolution, the sequence from a star's birth in a cool, dense cloud to its death.

Although these stars formed at the same time, their different masses will send them down very different paths. Tau Canis Majoris belongs to one of the most massive, short-lived types of star, so it will use up its fuel long before its smaller neighbours, which will keep shining for billions of years.
explore: The image was made for the ESO Cosmic Gems programme, which uses telescope time unsuitable for science to create images for education and outreach. Its data are still archived for astronomers. The cluster lies about 5000 light-years away.

caption: The light echo around V838 Monocerotis, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image, taken on 2 September 2002, shows light echoing through space around the star V838 Monocerotis. It is picture two of a four-part series made with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

The echo was set off by an unusual outburst of the star in January 2002. A light echo happens when a flash of light from a star travels outward and reflects off surrounding dust. Light that bounces off dust farther from the star takes longer to reach us, so over time we see different layers of dust lit up in turn, giving the impression of an expanding shell.

By taking a sequence of pictures, astronomers could watch the echo unfold, making the sequence a dramatic demonstration of this effect. The star at the centre remains something of a mystery, as its erupting behaviour was unusual. This frame captures one step in that changing view, some months after the outburst began.
explore: The picture combines exposures through blue, green and infrared filters. The star lies about 20,000 light-years away.

caption: The binary star Mira and its heart-shaped bubble, imaged by ALMA
story: A heart-shaped bubble sits at the centre of this ALMA image, part of a complex nebula around the binary star system Mira. Mira A ranks among the sky's best-known red giants, an old star already throwing the products of its life back into space to be recycled.

Its companion, Mira B, orbits it at twice the distance between the Sun and Neptune. Mira A has a slow wind that gently shapes the material around it. ALMA confirmed that Mira B is a very different star: a hot, dense white dwarf with a fierce, fast wind. The heart-shaped bubble is blown by Mira B's energetic wind inside Mira A's calmer outflow, and it formed within roughly the last 400 years.

Studying red giants tells astronomers about the Sun's future and how earlier stars spread the elements needed for life. Mira shows how double stars can shape their surroundings differently from single stars like the Sun.
explore: Other old, dying stars also have strange surroundings, but it is not always clear whether they are single or double. Mira's two stars have strongly affected each other despite their separation, leaving clues for scientists to decode.

caption: The brown dwarf VVV BD001, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: At the very centre of this VISTA image sits a newly discovered brown dwarf nicknamed VVV BD001. It lies about 55 light-years away, in the direction of our galaxy's densely packed centre, and it was the first new brown dwarf found in our cosmic neighbourhood by the VVV Survey.

Brown dwarfs are often called failed stars. They form the way stars do, but lack the mass to ignite hydrogen burning. They are larger than planets like Jupiter, yet smaller than stars. Being much cooler and dimmer, they are hard to find. Astronomers usually hunt them with infrared cameras and avoid crowded areas like the galactic centre.

That makes VVV BD001 doubly odd. It is the first found towards the Milky Way's centre, and it belongs to a class called unusually blue brown dwarfs. Why such objects are bluer than expected is still unclear. It turned up by chance during the survey.
explore: VISTA, at ESO's Paranal Observatory, is described as the world's largest survey telescope. Its VVV survey aims to catalogue a billion objects in the Milky Way's centre, and its data have produced a 3D map of the bulge and an image of nearly nine billion pixels.

caption: The globular cluster ESO 520-21, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Somewhere in this glittering field of stars is ESO 520-21, a globular cluster that also goes by Palomar 6, photographed with two of Hubble's cameras. A globular cluster is a densely packed, roughly spherical collection of stars.

ESO 520-21 sits near our galaxy's centre, where gas and dust between the stars absorb starlight and make observing harder. That absorption affects some wavelengths more than others, so objects look redder than they really are. Astronomers call this reddening, and it makes it particularly hard to work out the properties of clusters near the galactic centre.

The cluster sits in Ophiuchus, near the celestial equator. Ptolemy, an Egyptian astronomer of the second century, listed Ophiuchus among his 48 constellations, and all 48 still feature in the International Astronomical Union's official list of 88. Not every constellation survived history, though: forgotten ones include Felis the Cat and Rangifer the Reindeer.
explore: Another abandoned constellation was Officina Typographica, the Printer's Workshop. The image is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and R. Cohen.

caption: The globular cluster Messier 75, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble shows Messier 75, a globular cluster, which is a round swarm of stars held together by their own gravity. Such clusters circle galaxies and usually keep to the quieter outer regions, forming tight-knit communities far from the busy centre.

The cluster lies in Sagittarius, the Archer, around 67,000 light-years from Earth. Most of its roughly 400 000 stars crowd into the core, making it among the most densely populated clusters known, and together they shine some 180 000 times as brightly as the Sun, which helps explain why it photographs so well.

Pierre Méchain discovered Messier 75 in 1780. Charles Messier observed it too and added it to his famous catalogue later that same year. Today it is known as one of the most densely populated globular clusters ever found.
explore: This image was captured with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, and its data listing also includes the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2. It is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and F. Ferraro and colleagues.
