caption: The globular cluster NGC 1854, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: White and blue stars gather in this Hubble image of NGC 1854, a globular cluster in the southern constellation of Dorado, the Dolphinfish. Its home, about 135 000 light-years away, is the Large Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way and one of our nearest cosmic neighbours.

Stars are forming vigorously across the Large Magellanic Cloud. Well stocked with gas and dust, it holds approximately 60 globular clusters and 700 open clusters. Together with its smaller sibling, the Small Magellanic Cloud, it is the only system known to contain clusters at every stage of evolution, which makes its clusters popular subjects for research.

Hubble is often called on to study them. Its very high-resolution cameras can pick out individual stars even in a cluster's crowded core, revealing each cluster's mass, size and how far it has evolved. That lets astronomers compare clusters of many different ages side by side.
explore: The caption gives a distance of about 135 000 light-years, while catalogue data lists about 140,000 light-years. The image comes from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 6723, imaged by ESO's VISTA telescope
story: It may look like snow falling on a winter's night, but this is NGC 6723, a globular cluster in Sagittarius, seen in infrared light, taken with ESO's VISTA telescope at Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Globular clusters are spherical groups of stars bound tightly by gravity. The name comes from the Latin globulus, small sphere, which undersells clusters like NGC 6723 that hold hundreds of thousands to millions of stars. Astronomers have found more than 150 in the Milky Way, most thought to be 10 billion years old or more and hosting some of the galaxy's oldest stars.

These clusters also helped us find our place in the galaxy. Early in the 20th century, the American astronomer Harlow Shapley worked out how far away several of them were, and noticed they formed a roughly spherical spread with the Sun off-centre. He correctly concluded that the Milky Way's heart lies at the centre of that spread, putting the Sun in the galactic suburbs.
explore: The image is credited to ESO and S. Meingast and colleagues, and was taken with VISTA's VIRCAM camera.

caption: The open star cluster NGC 299, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble captures NGC 299, an open star cluster sitting in the Small Magellanic Cloud a little less than 200,000 light-years from us. It lies in the southern constellation of Tucana, the Toucan, famous for the Tucana Dwarf Galaxy and the cluster 47 Tucanae, but home to many quieter beauties too.

Open clusters are collections of stars weakly held together by gravity, all born from a single large cloud of molecular gas and dust. As a result, the stars share the same age and composition. They differ in mass, though, because they formed in different parts of the cloud.

That combination is what makes such a cluster valuable. With age and composition fixed, astronomers can see how mass alone shapes a star's life, since the way stars form and evolve is thought to depend strongly on their mass. The cluster becomes a natural laboratory, and seen through an instrument like Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, a striking one.
explore: 47 Tucanae, also in Tucana, is the second-brightest globular cluster in the night sky.

caption: The globular cluster Terzan 9, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Stars are strewn so thickly across this Hubble image that it looks like a sea of sequins, or a treasure chest overflowing with gold. At its heart is Terzan 9, a globular cluster in Sagittarius, in the direction of the Milky Way's centre.

Globular clusters are stable, tightly bound gatherings of anywhere from tens of thousands to millions of stars, and their cores can be extremely crowded, as this view shows. Hubble recorded the scene with two cameras, Wide Field Camera 3 and the Advanced Camera for Surveys.

The picture is part of a Hubble programme looking at globular clusters towards our galaxy's heart. That central region holds a dense crowd of stars called the Galactic bulge, which is also full of dust. The dust has long made nearby clusters hard to study, because it soaks up starlight and can shift the apparent colours of their stars. By observing in both visible and infrared light, Hubble lets astronomers measure how much the dust has altered those colours, and so work out the clusters' ages.
explore: The image is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and R. Cohen.

caption: The irregular galaxy UGC 12682, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing warmly against a dark background, the irregular galaxy UGC 12682 looks distorted and oddly structured in this Hubble image, dotted with bright pockets where stars are forming. It lies approximately 70 million light-years away in Pegasus, the Winged Horse.

In November 2008, a 14-year-old from New York, Caroline Moore, discovered a supernova in this galaxy, becoming at the time the youngest person ever to find one. Professional follow-up observations showed that the explosion, named SN 2008ha, was odd in several ways. Its host galaxy rarely produces supernovae. It was one of the faintest supernovae ever seen, and it expanded very slowly afterwards, suggesting the blast released far less energy than expected.

Astronomers now classify SN 2008ha as a subclass of Type Ia supernova, the explosion of a white dwarf that has been pulling matter from a companion star. It may have been a partly failed supernova, which could explain why it did not destroy the whole star.
explore: A white dwarf is the dense leftover core of a star like the Sun. The image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3.

caption: The Wolf-Rayet star WR 31a and its blue bubble, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: A distinctive blue bubble seems to surround a sparkling star at the centre of this Hubble image. The star is WR 31a, a Wolf-Rayet star about 30,000 light-years away in Carina, the Keel, and it has an uncatalogued companion. The bubble is a Wolf-Rayet nebula, a cloud of dust, hydrogen, helium and other gases.

Such nebulae form when fast stellar winds collide with the outer layers of hydrogen that Wolf-Rayet stars have thrown off, and they are often ring-shaped or spherical. This bubble is thought to be around 20 000 years old, and it is growing at around 220 000 kilometres per hour.

Wolf-Rayet stars do not last long, just a few hundred thousand years, a brief moment in cosmic terms. They start out with at least 20 times the Sun's mass but typically lose half of it in under 100 000 years. WR 31a will eventually explode as a supernova, and its scattered material will later feed new stars and planets.
explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with an acknowledgement to Judy Schmidt.

caption: The star cluster Pismis 24 in the nebula NGC 6357, imaged by the Danish 1.54-metre telescope at La Silla
story: Blazing at the heart of NGC 6357, a nebula in Scorpius, the Scorpion, is the open star cluster Pismis 24. The surrounding clouds take on strange shapes and give the image a hazy look.

Pismis 24 is home to some of the largest stars ever found. Several of its members weigh more than 100 times the mass of the Sun, true monster stars. These huge, hot stars pour out enormous amounts of fierce radiation, and it is that radiation that sculpts the odd shapes of the surrounding clouds.

The nebula also keeps secrets. Its gas and dust hide huge young stars from telescopes that observe in visible light, and they add to the haze across the picture. The image was made through three visible-light filters, B, V and R, with the Danish 1.5-metre telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile. Seeing the hidden young stars would require wavelengths that pass through dust more easily.
explore: Pismis 24 lies about 8000 light-years away. The image is credited to ESO, IDA, the Danish 1.5-metre telescope team, R. Gendler, U.G. Jørgensen, J. Skottfelt and K. Harpsøe.

caption: The young star IRAS 12196-6300 and its reflection nebulae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: At the centre of this Hubble image is IRAS 12196-6300, an emission-line star just under 2300 light-years from Earth. Hazy clouds float above and below it.

Spread its light into a spectrum and you get a rainbow of colours crossed by a pattern of bright and dark lines. Each kind of atom and molecule leaves its own set of lines, like a fingerprint, so comparing them reveals what the star is made of. In this star, the emission lines are especially prominent.

IRAS 12196-6300 is still in its infancy: under 10 million years old, and, unlike the Sun, not yet burning hydrogen in its core. The hazy clouds are more evidence of its youth. They are reflection nebulae, formed when starlight bounces off a dense concentration of dust. Here that dust is probably material left over from the star's own formation, still lingering around it.
explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys, with an acknowledgement to Judy Schmidt (Geckzilla).

caption: The nebula around the star AG Carinae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This comparison view presents two versions of the nebula around the giant star AG Carinae. One highlights glowing ionised hydrogen and nitrogen, shown in red as a thick, bright ring that looks doubled in places. The other shows dust, in blue, formed into clumps, bubbles and filaments shaped by the star's wind.

AG Carinae is a Luminous Blue Variable: hot, extremely bright and changeable. Such stars are rare, since few stars are so massive. Late in life they shed mass continuously, throwing material into space until they settle. AG Carinae is locked in a tug-of-war between gravity and radiation to avoid tearing itself apart.

Its nebula, about five light-years wide, is roughly 10 000 years old and built from past outbursts. It looks like a ring but is really a hollow shell, cleared in the middle by a stellar wind of roughly 200 kilometres per second. The doubled parts may be outbursts that collided.
explore: The shell is not perfectly spherical but shows a two-sided symmetry. That might point to a central disc, an unseen companion star, or, more simply, a very fast spin. The gas moves at about 70 kilometres per second.

caption: The star cluster NGC 602 in the Wing of the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by Chandra, Hubble and Spitzer
story: This composite from NASA's Great Observatories shows the cluster NGC 602 and its surroundings in the Wing, a region of the Small Magellanic Cloud, which orbits the Milky Way. Chandra's X-ray data appear in purple, Hubble's visible light in red, green and blue, and Spitzer's infrared data in red.

Chandra made the first detection of X-rays from young Sun-like stars outside our galaxy here. X-rays from young stars reveal how active their magnetic fields are, and magnetic activity offers clues to how fast a star spins and how hot gas rises and falls inside it.

Astronomers suggest that if young stars have similar X-ray properties in very different environments, then related properties, such as how planets form around them, are likely to be similar too. Studying young stars in another galaxy therefore helps astronomers test whether stars and planets form the same way in very different surroundings.
explore: The Wing is a region of the Small Magellanic Cloud. Credits: X-ray, NASA/CXC/Univ. Potsdam/L. Oskinova and colleagues; optical, ESA and NASA/STScI; infrared, NASA/JPL-Caltech.

understand.summary: The image combines Chandra X-rays (shown in purple), Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys visible and hydrogen-alpha light (in red, green and blue), and Spitzer IRAC infrared data (in red).
understand.eye: X-rays and infrared light are both invisible to the eye, so much of this picture shows light we could never see directly.

caption: The Crab pulsar, imaged by the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This image comes from an unusual project: a space movie made by two of NASA's Great Observatories. Over several months, the Chandra X-ray Observatory and the Hubble Space Telescope observed the Crab pulsar again and again, and the sequence of images was assembled to show change over time.

A pulsar is a kind of neutron star, the collapsed core left behind after a massive star explodes. The Crab pulsar spins rapidly, and it is astonishingly compact: the collapsed remnant is only about the size of Manhattan.

What the observations captured was dramatic. The pulsar hurls matter and antimatter outward at close to the speed of light. By watching the region repeatedly, astronomers could follow how this outflow behaves rather than seeing a single frozen moment, which is why the project was billed as an action movie. This still offers one frame of that activity.
explore: The Crab pulsar lies about 6000 light-years away. Credits go to NASA/CXC/ASU/J. Hester and colleagues for the X-ray data and HST/ASU/J. Hester and colleagues for the Hubble data.

understand.summary: The observations combine X-ray data from Chandra with Hubble images. The source does not list filters or publish a colour mapping.
understand.eye: X-rays are invisible to the eye, and the changes shown unfolded over months, far too slowly to watch directly.

alt: The region around the Crab pulsar, a rapidly spinning neutron star, as seen by Chandra and Hubble.

caption: The planetary nebula NGC 2818 in the open cluster NGC 2818A, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Glowing clouds of gas in red, green and blue make up NGC 2818, a planetary nebula nested inside the open star cluster NGC 2818A, in the southern constellation Pyxis, the Compass. Few other planetary nebulae in the Milky Way are known to lie inside an open cluster.

That is rare for a reason. Open clusters are loosely bound and drift apart over hundreds of millions of years, while stars that make planetary nebulae usually live for billions. This cluster is unusually old, estimated at nearly a billion years. The nebula is the outer layers of a Sun-like star, cast off once it ran out of fuel for the nuclear reactions in its core.

NGC 2818's complex shape is hard to interpret, but because it lies in the cluster, astronomers can learn its age and distance. Such nebulae fade over tens of thousands of years, and the Sun will go the same way in about 5 billion years.
explore: The star's hot remnant core will cool for billions of years as a white dwarf. The nebula is also catalogued as PLN 261+8.1. The caption puts the pair over 10 000 light-years away, while catalogue data lists about 7500.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the nebula through narrow filters: red represents nitrogen, green hydrogen, and blue oxygen.
understand.eye: The colours isolate light from individual gases, a separation the eye cannot make.

alt: A complex planetary nebula of glowing red, green and blue gas inside a star cluster.

caption: White dwarfs in the globular cluster Messier 4, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble peers deep into Messier 4, a globular cluster of several hundred thousand stars. Hidden among them, it found the oldest burned-out stars known in the Milky Way.

These are white dwarfs, the small, dying remains of stars that have used up their fuel. White dwarfs cool and fade at a steady rate, so how dim they have become works like a clock. The ancient white dwarfs in Messier 4 turn out to be about 12 to 13 billion years old.

That makes them useful for one of astronomy's biggest questions: how old is the Universe? Astronomers allowed for the time the cluster took to form after the Big Bang, and found that the white dwarfs' age agrees with earlier estimates of the Universe's age. The white dwarfs thus offer another way of reading the age of the Universe.
explore: Messier 4 lies about 5500 light-years away. The image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 and is credited to NASA/ESA and H. Richer.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the cluster through ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: White dwarfs are extremely faint, far beyond what the eye could detect, and part of the data is ultraviolet and near-infrared light we cannot see.

alt: A dense field of stars deep inside a globular cluster.

caption: A star field in Crux, the Southern Cross, imaged by ESO's Very Large Telescope
story: Stars of every age crowd this image from ESO's Very Large Telescope, some close by in the foreground and others far in the distance. Their distinct red and blue hues come from the way the picture was made. The patch of sky lies in Crux, the Southern Cross, an extremely bright stretch of the Milky Way.

Astronomical cameras record light in shades of grey, so colour pictures like this are built from several images taken through different filters, each letting through a particular range of wavelengths. Each filtered image is given its own colour, and the separate images are then combined. The result represents the different wavelengths of light in colour.

The picture was taken with the FORS instrument, short for FOcal Reducer and low dispersion Spectrograph. It was made for the ESO Cosmic Gems programme, which produces images of interesting or attractive objects for education and public outreach.
explore: Cosmic Gems runs on telescope time that is unsuitable for scientific work. Even so, the data may be scientifically useful, so they are made available to astronomers through ESO's science archive.

understand.summary: The FORS2 instrument on the Very Large Telescope imaged this field through blue, visual, red and hydrogen-alpha filters, each assigned its own colour before combining. The source does not publish which colour was given to each filter.
understand.eye: The colours come from filters and processing choices, and the telescope's exposures reveal far more distant, faint stars than the eye could see.

caption: The globular cluster 47 Tucanae (NGC 104), imaged by ESO's 1-metre Schmidt Telescope
story: This colour-corrected image shows NGC 104, better known as 47 Tucanae, the second-largest and second-brightest globular cluster in Earth's night sky. A globular cluster is a tight, roughly spherical grouping of stars bound together by gravity, and this one is a tight grouping of a great many stars.

The light for the picture was gathered in 1986 with ESO's 1-metre Schmidt Telescope at La Silla Observatory in Chile. A Schmidt telescope is designed to photograph wide areas of sky at once, which makes it well suited to capturing a large, bright cluster like this in a single frame.

The telescope has since been decommissioned, so this image is also a small piece of observatory history. It records the cluster as the Schmidt Telescope saw it, a snapshot from an instrument that no longer observes.
explore: 47 Tucanae lies about 15,000 light-years from Earth.

understand.summary: This is a colour-corrected visible-light image from ESO's 1-metre Schmidt Telescope. The source does not list the filters or publish the colour mapping.
understand.eye: The telescope gathers far more light than the eye, recording stars too faint to see directly.

alt: A large, bright globular cluster of densely packed stars.

caption: Dust rings around the binary star Wolf-Rayet 140, imaged by the James Webb Space Telescope
story: At least 17 pink-orange rings spread out like ripples from a pair of bright stars at the centre of this Webb image, set against black space scattered with tiny red galaxies. The pair is known as Wolf-Rayet 140.

Each ring formed when the two stars swung close and their stellar winds collided, compressing gas into dust. Their orbit brings them together about once every eight years, so, like tree rings, the dust loops keep time. The orbit is elongated; only when the stars come about as close as Earth is to the Sun is the gas squeezed enough to make dust.

One star is a Wolf-Rayet star, born with at least 25 times the Sun's mass and nearing its end. Its powerful winds carry carbon from deep inside, which cools and is kneaded into dust where the winds meet. This study gives the best evidence yet that such stars make carbon-rich dust that survives between the stars.
explore: Webb's MIRI instrument sees the longest infrared wavelengths, ideal for cool dust. Astronomers expect a few thousand Wolf-Rayet stars in our galaxy, but only about 600 have been found. Swept-up material around them may help form new stars, and there is some evidence the Sun formed that way.

understand.summary: Webb's Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) imaged the rings at 7.7 microns (shown in blue), 15 microns (green) and 21 microns (red).
understand.eye: Webb detects infrared light, which the human eye cannot see, so the colours are a translation of mid-infrared wavelengths.

scaleExtra: The pair lies just over 5000 light-years from Earth, according to the release.

caption: Stars near the centre of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: Hubble zooms in on 35 000 stars swarming close to the central region of the globular cluster 47 Tucanae. The stars here are packed together far more tightly than the Sun and its nearest stellar neighbours.

The picture, taken with the Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2, shows the stars in their natural colours, and those colours carry information about each star's make-up and age. Red stars here are bright red giants approaching the ends of their lives, while the more numerous yellow ones resemble the Sun, which is in middle age.
That makes the picture more than a pretty view. By reading the colours of so many individual stars at once, scientists can learn about the make-up and age of the cluster's population.
explore: 47 Tucanae lies about 15,000 light-years away. The image is credited to Ron Gilliland of the Space Telescope Science Institute and NASA/ESA.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field and Planetary Camera 2 imaged the stars through ultraviolet, visible and near-infrared filters, and ESA/Hubble describes the result as showing the stars' natural colours. The source does not publish the exact colour assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is ultraviolet and near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see.

alt: A dense swarm of red and yellow stars near the centre of a globular cluster.

caption: The globular cluster NGC 3201, imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope
story: This colour composite shows the globular cluster NGC 3201, captured with the Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope at La Silla. It lies about 16 000 light-years away, towards the southern constellation of Vela.

Globular clusters are large, densely packed swarms of stars, some containing up to millions of members. They are among the oldest objects astronomers observe, and are presumed to be roughly as old as the Milky Way itself, dating from the early period after the Big Bang. That makes them valuable windows into our galaxy's distant past.

The data were collected for the ESO Imaging Survey, a public survey run by ESO and its member states to prepare for first light of the Very Large Telescope. First light is the moment a new telescope begins observing, and this survey was carried out in preparation for that milestone.
explore: The original image and data were released through the survey's Pre-Flames data pages. The caption gives a distance of about 16 000 light-years, while catalogue data lists about 15,000.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-metre telescope imaged the cluster through blue, visual and near-infrared filters. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: Part of the data is near-infrared light, which the eye cannot see, and the long exposures gather far more light than any eye.

caption: The open cluster NGC 2477, imaged for ESO by J. Pérez
story: This image shows NGC 2477, also known as Caldwell 71, an open star cluster in the constellation Puppis. It holds about 300 stars and spreads across a patch of sky almost as large as the full Moon.

An open cluster is a group of stars that formed together from the same cloud and are only loosely held by gravity. Estimates put NGC 2477 at about 700 million years old. Because its members share a birthplace, they also share an age, which is how astronomers can speak of the age of the cluster as a whole.

Observers rate it highly, ranking it among the finest open clusters to be seen. It looks rather like a well-resolved globular cluster, but without the dense, crowded centre that globular clusters have. Abbé Lacaille discovered it in 1751.
explore: The image is credited to ESO and J. Pérez; the source does not name the telescope or instrument used.

understand.summary: The source does not name the telescope, filters or colour mapping for this image.
understand.eye: A camera's long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing many more of the cluster's fainter stars.

alt: A broad open cluster of many stars.

caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 1309, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
story: This Hubble image shows the spiral galaxy NGC 1309. A spiral galaxy is a flat, rotating disc of stars, gas and dust, with arms that wind out from a central bulge, much like our own Milky Way.

NGC 1309 is notable for something that happened in its outskirts. Astronomers observed a rare type of stellar explosion there, a Type Iax supernova, catalogued as Supernova 2012Z. Its position is marked in a separate, annotated version of the image released alongside this one.

Supernovae are among the most powerful events in the Universe, and a single one can briefly shine as brightly as a large part of its host galaxy. Type Iax explosions are an unusual variety, which is why this one drew attention. This picture shows the galaxy that hosted it.
explore: NGC 1309 lies about 100 million light-years away. The image is credited to NASA, ESA, the Hubble Heritage Team and A. Riess.

understand.summary: The source does not list the Hubble instrument, filters or colour mapping for this image.
understand.eye: The galaxy is far too faint to see without a telescope, and Hubble's long exposures reveal detail no eye could.

alt: A spiral galaxy seen by Hubble.

caption: Green-lit ALMA antennas under the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: The antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array seem to glow an eerie, vivid green in this photograph from the Chajnantor plateau, high in Chile's Atacama Desert. It could almost be a landing site for friendly aliens, but the explanation is ordinary: indicator lights on the antennas tell staff whether it is safe to approach, and green means yes.

Above them, the clear Chilean sky holds the band of the Milky Way. In the top left, two bright stars sit side by side. They are often called the Pointers, because they lead the eye to the bright diamond shape of the Southern Cross immediately to their right.

The one closer to the Southern Cross is Beta Centauri, some 400 light-years away. The other is Alpha Centauri, the nearest star system to the Sun at just 4.37 light-years. It includes the red dwarf Proxima Centauri, where in 2016 astronomers using ESO telescopes found evidence of an Earth-sized planet in the habitable zone.
explore: ESO is a partner in ALMA, which stands on the isolated Chajnantor plateau in Chile's Atacama Desert.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at the ALMA site; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: The camera records the Milky Way far more vividly than the eye would see it.

alt: ALMA antennas glowing with green indicator lights under a sky with the Milky Way and two bright stars at the top left.

caption: The Moon, Saturn and Mercury over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Looking west from ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile, this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek centres on the bright Moon, with ringed Saturn a little way to its upper left and rocky Mercury off to its lower left. From some latitudes, this close pairing of the two planets is tricky to pick out by eye, yet here both show clearly despite the Moon's glare.

The dusty band of the Milky Way seems to split the sky horizontally, with a star-filled night above and the last traces of sunset below. Several well-known nebulae appear along this band, including the Lagoon Nebula, the Cat's Paw Nebula and the Trifid Nebula.

Below the sky stand the individual telescopes that together make up ESO's Very Large Telescope. Its four big Unit Telescopes have mirrors 8.2 metres wide, joined by four smaller Auxiliary Telescopes whose mirrors measure 1.8 metres.
explore: ESO describes the VLT as the world's most advanced optical and infrared observatory.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: The camera brings out the Milky Way and its nebulae more strongly than the eye would see them, especially with the Moon so bright.

alt: The Moon with Saturn and Mercury nearby, above the band of the Milky Way and the telescopes of Paranal, with fading sunset light below.

caption: A meteor falling over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: A spectacular streak of light slices across the sky above the ALMA antennas in this photograph, glowing emerald green, gold and faint crimson. It is a meteor, a shooting star, burning up as it enters Earth's atmosphere. Near the centre of the image, Spica, the brightest star in Virgo, and the planet Mars shine as they rise above the horizon.

The fireball is really a small grain of rock from interplanetary space. As it plunges into the air it heats up, and its outer layers vaporise, leaving a glowing trail that vanishes within seconds. The camera caught it in a moment.

Some of ALMA's 66 high-precision antennas point skyward, studying cold clouds between the stars and looking far back towards our cosmic origins. The array sits 5000 metres above sea level on the remote Chajnantor plateau in the Chilean Andes. The photo was taken during a time-lapse sequence for the ESO Ultra HD Expedition.
explore: The photographer was Christoph Malin, an ESO Photo Ambassador who specialises in time-lapse, working on the team's eighth night at Chajnantor. The expedition, which began in Santiago, also included Herbert Zodet, Yuri Beletsky and Babak Tafreshi.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph from a time-lapse sequence shot with Ultra HD camera equipment; the source gives no exposure settings.
understand.eye: A meteor lasts only seconds, and the camera freezes and records its colours and the surrounding sky more vividly than the eye could.

alt: A bright green, gold and crimson meteor streak above ALMA antennas, with a bright star and Mars near the centre.

caption: Airglow and the Milky Way over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stand guard beneath a star-filled sky in this view of Paranal Observatory. The glittering arch of our galaxy spans the scene, the glowing Magellanic Clouds sit on the left, and soft swathes of green, yellow, red and orange lie close to the horizon.

Chile's Atacama Desert is one of the darkest, quietest astronomical sites on Earth, which is why ESO has built its observatories there. Yet as this picture shows, even Paranal's sky is not completely dark. After sunset, Earth's own atmosphere glows in many hues, painting the sky like a watercolour.

That colourful wash is airglow, a faint light produced by chemical processes up to a few hundred kilometres above the ground. It joins the distant emission nebulae dotting the Milky Way and the constellation of Orion in the upper centre. At lower centre, a diffuse white ray is sunlight reflecting off specks of rock and ice between the Sun and us.
explore: The Sun had only just set in the west, at the centre of the frame, when the picture was taken, which is why its light still catches those specks of rock and ice.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: The camera brings out the colours of the airglow and the Milky Way more strongly than the eye would see them.

alt: VLT telescopes under an arching Milky Way, with the Magellanic Clouds on the left and bands of green, yellow, red and orange airglow near the horizon.

caption: The Residencia under the night sky, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Starlight falls across flowing desert dunes and the Residencia, the residence building at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile. Light pollution is practically absent at this remote site high in the Atacama Desert, so even after sunset the landscape is lit by the stars above. The only artificial lights for miles come from Paranal's own facilities, the telescopes and this building among them.

The Residencia is a true oasis. Astronomers and other staff who work at the observatory, which lies a short drive away and houses the Very Large Telescope, can come here after a long shift to escape the dry desert air, stroll through an indoor garden or take a swim in the pool.

The building is known for its striking design and its environmental innovations, including careful management of power and waste. A huge 35-metre glass dome on its roof lets natural starlight and sunlight pour into the building. And the view from its windows, as this photograph suggests, is rather good.
explore: The photograph is credited to ESO and P. Horálek.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure gathers far more starlight than the eye, so the stars and the starlit landscape look brighter here than they would in person.

alt: The Residencia building among desert dunes under a starry night sky.

caption: ALMA antennas beneath the Milky Way, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Several antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array point skyward beneath a panoramic view of the centre of the Milky Way. Crux, the Southern Cross, sits a little above the closest antenna and to its right, and a little further right lies the Carina Nebula. Green lights glow on the antennas.
Those lights are a normal part of how the telescopes operate, though here they lend the Chilean site an ethereal, otherworldly air.

This photograph shows only part of ALMA. The full array is made of 66 individual antennas and can spread out over distances of up to 16 kilometres. Working together, the antennas act as one enormous telescope. Astronomers use ALMA to look inside gigantic molecular clouds where stars are forming, and to watch young galaxies taking shape at the farthest reaches of the observable Universe.
explore: ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek took the photograph.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken with a camera at the ALMA site; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: The camera's exposure records the Milky Way's centre much more vividly than the eye would see it.

alt: ALMA antennas with green lights beneath the Milky Way, with the Southern Cross and Carina Nebula to the right.

caption: The Gegenschein above the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A faint band of light runs diagonally from the top left to the lower right of this night sky over Paranal, home of ESO's Very Large Telescope. It is the Gegenschein, German for counter shine, a famous and extremely hard-to-observe glow that Paranal's very dark sky reveals here in full.

The Gegenschein is a faint brightening of the night sky along the ecliptic, the Sun's path across the sky, at the point directly opposite the Sun. It is caused by interplanetary dust in the Solar System reflecting sunlight back towards us.

Yuri Beletsky took the image in October 2007 with a digital camera fitted with a 10-mm wide-angle lens on a portable equatorial mount, which follows the stars as Earth turns. The total exposure lasted about 45 minutes. Conditions were excellent and the sky almost perfectly transparent, letting him record the glow's faintest details and bring out its fine structure.
explore: The image is also sold as a mounted print in the ESOshop.

understand.summary: This is a wide-angle photograph from a digital camera on a tracking mount, with a total exposure of about 45 minutes, as stated by ESO.
understand.eye: The Gegenschein is extremely faint; the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, revealing structure no observer could see directly.

alt: A starry night sky over Paranal with a faint diagonal band of light running from top left to lower right.

caption: Jupiter, the Milky Way and a laser over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A wide band of stars and dust clouds, the Milky Way, arcs across more than 100 degrees of sky above Paranal in this photograph by ESO astronomer Yuri Beletsky, taken on 21 July 2007. At the centre, two bright objects stand out: the brighter is the planet Jupiter, and the other is the star Antares.

Below, three of the four 8.2-metre telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope are visible. A laser beam shoots out of Yepun, Unit Telescope number 4, aimed straight at the centre of our galaxy. Three of the smaller 1.8-metre Auxiliary Telescopes, used for interferometry, also appear, marked by small beams of light from diodes on their domes.

The exposure lasted five minutes. Because the camera tracked the stars as they moved across the sky, the telescopes on the ground are slightly blurred. It is a neat reminder that the sky turns overhead while the observatory stays fixed.
explore: Interferometry combines light from several telescopes so they can work together to see finer detail than any single one.

understand.summary: This is a photograph with a five-minute exposure, tracked on the stars, as stated by ESO; the source gives no other camera details.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, so the Milky Way's dust clouds and stars look richer than they would in person.

alt: The Milky Way arching over three VLT telescopes, one firing a laser, with Jupiter and Antares bright at the centre.

caption: A laser aimed at the galactic centre from the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Two of the 8.2-metre telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope stand against the myriad stars and dust of the Milky Way in this view of the sky above Paranal on 21 July 2007. Just above Yepun, Unit Telescope number 4, shines the Small Magellanic Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way.

A laser beam streams out of Yepun towards the centre of our galaxy. It serves a practical purpose: it helps the telescope obtain images free from the blurring caused by Earth's atmosphere. In this picture the beam looks slightly artificial, a side effect of saturation during the long exposure.

The brightest object, at upper right, is the planet Jupiter, sitting next to the star Antares. The image was taken by ESO astronomer Yuri Beletsky. It shows a working observatory in action under the night sky.
explore: Saturation happens when a camera receives more light than it can record, so the brightest parts of an image lose detail.

understand.summary: This is a long-exposure photograph of the sky over Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details beyond that.
understand.eye: The long exposure gathers far more light than the eye, and saturation makes the laser beam look slightly artificial.

alt: Two VLT telescopes under the Milky Way, one firing a laser beam, with the Small Magellanic Cloud above and Jupiter bright at upper right.

caption: One hour of satellite trails above the Extremely Large Telescope, northern Atacama Desert, Chile
story: Many bright streaks cross the night sky above Chile's northern Atacama Desert in this image. It is a stack of frames from a time-lapse video filmed on 15 October 2025, starting roughly two hours after the Sun went down, and together they show the traffic overhead during just one hour.

A few of the trails were made by aeroplanes, easy to recognise from their blinking coloured lights. Most, though, are satellites crossing the sky. Each satellite catches sunlight and leaves a line across the frame as it moves, and stacking an hour's worth of frames shows how many pass over.

In the foreground stands the dome of ESO's Extremely Large Telescope, described as the world's largest optical and infrared telescope, still under construction on Cerro Armazones. Behind it, the lasers of ESO's Very Large Telescope shine from Paranal Observatory, 22 kilometres away. The scene gives a sense of how much traffic crosses the sky above these remote observatories in a single hour.
explore: The image is credited to F. Kamphues and ESO/M. Kornmesser.

understand.summary: This is a stack of frames from a time-lapse video covering one hour, as stated by ESO; the source gives no camera details.
understand.eye: Stacking an hour of frames shows every trail at once, whereas the eye would see each satellite only as a single moving point.

alt: Many bright satellite trails across the night sky above the ELT dome, with laser beams from the distant VLT behind it.

caption: The Milky Way above the Very Large Telescope Interferometer, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: The Milky Way stretches grandly across this photograph from Paranal, with the Magellanic Clouds visible on the right. The foreground shows several of the docking stations used by the Auxiliary Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope Interferometer.

Almost at the centre of the image shines Alpha Centauri, the lower of the two Pointers that lead to the Southern Cross. They sit just above the dark patch known as the Coal Sack, a cloud of dust that blocks the light of the stars behind it. The photo looks towards the east.

There is a bonus, too: a shooting star streaks across the top right of the frame, caught in the brief moment it burned up. The image was taken on 11 December 2005 by Hännes Heyer of ESO, using a Canon EOS 5D camera with exposures of 40 and 20 seconds. The docking stations let the movable Auxiliary Telescopes be placed in different positions.
explore: By moving the Auxiliary Telescopes between stations, astronomers can change how the interferometer combines their light.

understand.summary: This photograph was taken with a Canon EOS 5D using 40- and 20-second exposures, as stated by ESO.
understand.eye: The exposures gather more light than the eye, so the Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds look brighter than they would in person.

alt: The Milky Way and Magellanic Clouds over Paranal, with telescope docking stations in the foreground and a shooting star at the top right.

caption: The night sky over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This photograph looks up into the night sky over ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile's Atacama Desert. ESO notes that the superb sky here gives the observatory excellent observing conditions.

Clear, dark, steady skies matter enormously to astronomers. The less light pollution and the fewer clouds there are, the fainter the objects a telescope can detect. Sites in the Atacama are prized for exactly these qualities.

The picture was released alongside news about the Cherenkov Telescope Array, which will build its southern-hemisphere observatory at Paranal and so share this sky with ESO's telescopes. Cherenkov telescopes study the Universe in a very different way from optical ones: they catch the brief flashes of faint light produced when very high-energy gamma rays from space strike Earth's atmosphere. The photograph is best enjoyed simply as a portrait of the sky that both observatories will look into.

understand.summary: This is a landscape photograph taken at Paranal; the source gives no camera or exposure details.
understand.eye: A camera exposure collects far more light than the eye, so the sky appears richer than it would in person.

alt: The night sky over Paranal Observatory in the Atacama Desert.

caption: The colours of the night sky over Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: This photograph shows the night sky above ESO's Paranal Observatory, high in Chile's Atacama Desert. Its title speaks of the colours of night, and ESO notes that the superb sky here gives the observatory excellent observing conditions.

Those conditions are why observatories come to this desert. A dark sky with little light pollution and few clouds lets telescopes pick out very faint objects, and cameras on long exposures can record colours the eye usually misses.

The image accompanied news that the Cherenkov Telescope Array will place its southern-hemisphere observatory at Paranal, sharing the same sky. Cherenkov telescopes look for the fleeting glimmers of light created when very high-energy gamma rays from space collide with Earth's atmosphere, an indirect way of studying some of the most energetic processes in the cosmos. The photograph is best seen as a portrait of the sky that will host both observatories.

caption: Southern star trails over ALMA, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: Great whorls of stars swirl above ALMA, the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array, in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi. The pattern recalls van Gogh's Starry Night, or perhaps the view from a spaceship leaping into hyperspace.

In fact, the circles trace Earth's rotation, revealed by a long exposure. In the southern hemisphere, the stars seem to wheel around the south celestial pole, found in the faint constellation of Octans, the Octant, between the better-known Southern Cross and the Magellanic Clouds. Given a long enough exposure, each star draws its own circular trail. Some antennas look blurred because they were moving while observing during the shot.

The photo was taken on the Chajnantor plateau, 5000 metres up in the Chilean Andes, home of ALMA. ALMA studies the cool Universe: molecular gas and dust, and the relic radiation from the Big Bang. When this picture was released, it was still under construction, but early science had already begun.
explore: ALMA was planned to have 54 antennas 12 metres across plus twelve 7-metre antennas. Europe, North America and East Asia run it jointly with Chile, and it is led for Europe by ESO, for North America by NRAO and for East Asia by NAOJ.

caption: A bright Perseid meteor over the Very Large Telescope, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A bright meteor streaks over the platform of ESO's Very Large Telescope at Paranal. Reddish light from the Moon, setting just beyond the left edge of the frame, illuminates the scene. This shot, from the night of 13–14 August 2010, was hand-picked from 8000 exposures by ESO Photo Ambassador Stéphane Guisard, who ran three cameras taking time-lapse pictures over two nights.

The meteor belongs to the Perseid shower, which peaks every year in mid-August as Earth passes through debris left by Comet Swift-Tuttle. Most of the particles are smaller than a grain of sand and burn up in the atmosphere, leaving glowing trails.

The Perseids are best seen from the northern hemisphere, but Paranal's very dark skies let them be spotted from Chile too. The debris travels in parallel, yet perspective makes the meteors seem to spread from one point in Perseus, low on the horizon here and partly hidden by the telescope enclosures. That radiant gives the shower its name.
explore: According to the International Meteor Organization, the 2010 shower was above normal, peaking at over 100 meteors per hour under ideal conditions, but not spectacular. Many thousands of people watched worldwide, some for citizen science projects such as Meteorwatch.

caption: Orion over ALMA antennas at the ALMA Operations Support Facility, Chile
story: Orion, the Hunter, stands high in the Chilean night sky above three antennas of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array. The constellation is easy to recognise by its hourglass shape and the three bright stars of Orion's Belt at its centre. Seen from the southern hemisphere, Orion's sword appears above the Belt.
The middle star of the sword is really the Orion Nebula, one of the finest sights in the sky, whose fuzzy glow can be seen with the naked eye in good conditions.

These three antennas are a small part of ALMA's 66. The array combines their signals over distances of up to 16 kilometres into a single giant telescope, a technique called interferometry. It normally works 5000 metres up on the arid Chajnantor plateau, because water vapour and oxygen absorb the millimetre and submillimetre light ALMA observes. These antennas, though, were being tested at the lower Operations Support Facility, at 2900 metres, before moving up.
explore: Adrian Russell took the photograph and shared it in ESO's Your ESO Pictures Flickr group, from which the best images are chosen for the Picture of the Week. ALMA is run jointly by Europe, North America and East Asia together with Chile.

caption: A laser beam towards the Milky Way's centre, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: A laser beam crosses the southern sky towards the centre of the Milky Way in this wide-angle photograph from ESO's Paranal Observatory. ESO Photo Ambassador Yuri Beletsky took it in mid-August 2010, while astronomers were observing the galactic centre with the laser guide star facility on Yepun, a Unit Telescope of the Very Large Telescope.

The laser makes an artificial star 90 kilometres up, in Earth's mesosphere. Its colour is tuned to excite a layer of sodium atoms, thought to be left over from meteorites, which is why it matches sodium street lamps. The glowing spot acts as a reference for the adaptive optics system, which corrects the atmosphere's blurring and gives sharper observations.
That matters for the galactic core, where a supermassive black hole, circled closely by stars, is swallowing gas and dust. Sharper images let researchers monitor that region better.
explore: The photo covers about 180 degrees of sky. It was selected as Wikimedia Picture of the Year 2010, and was also Astronomy Picture of the Day on 6 September 2010.

caption: Star trails over the APEX telescope, Chajnantor plateau, Chile
story: It might look like abstract art, but this is a long-exposure photograph taken above the Chajnantor plateau, high in the Chilean Andes. As Earth turns, the stars of the Milky Way stretch into colourful streaks, and the telescope in the foreground takes on a dreamlike look.

The telescope is APEX, the Atacama Pathfinder Experiment, which stands 5000 metres above sea level. It is 12 metres across and collects millimetre and submillimetre light, which astronomers use to study everything from cold clouds of gas and dust where stars are born to some of the earliest, most distant galaxies.

APEX is a pathfinder for ALMA, built on the same plateau. The two complement each other: APEX's wider field of view lets it find many targets across large areas of sky, and ALMA's much sharper resolution lets it study them in detail. Both help astronomers learn how stars like those wheeling overhead come to form.
explore: The photographer, ESO Photo Ambassador Babak Tafreshi, also founded The World At Night, which pairs landmark sites with the night sky. APEX is run jointly by ESO, the Onsala Space Observatory and the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy.

caption: Yepun and the Milky Way, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Yepun, the fourth Unit Telescope of ESO's Very Large Telescope in Chile, seems to take a bite out of the colourful band of the Milky Way in this photograph. So what is our galaxy made of?

Mostly stars, planets, and plenty of gas and dust, all bound by gravity, plus a generous helping of dark matter. The Milky Way is a medium-sized disc with spiral arms, wrapped in an outer halo. The Solar System sits in one of the arms, some 25 000 light-years from the centre, so we see only part of the galaxy. Its core hides behind thick dust, concealing the supermassive black hole Sagittarius A*, first imaged in 2022.

Astronomers estimate the galaxy holds between 100 and 400 billion stars, and probably as many planets. Older stars dominate the inner regions, while the arms are packed with young stars born from giant clouds of gas and dust. Out in the halo are globular clusters of old stars and the remains of small galaxies the Milky Way has swallowed.
explore: Galaxies spin so fast that stars, gas and dust alone could not hold them together. Scientists think the Milky Way sits inside a vast halo of dark matter, probably ten times the mass of all its stars or more. Telescopes like the VLT help by probing how it affects visible matter.

caption: The nebula Gum 40 (IC 2872), imaged by the VLT Survey Telescope
story: Is it a playful fox, a skulking hyena, or the head of a chicken? This cloud of gas in the constellation Centaurus belongs to the much larger Running Chicken Nebula. Some see it as the chicken's head, others as its rear end. The image comes from the VLT Survey Telescope at ESO's Paranal Observatory in Chile.

Fun nicknames are popular, but they do not make for clear communication in an international science, so the nebula also carries two plainer names. In 1955, Australian astronomer Colin Stanley Gum listed 84 emission nebulae in the southern sky, and this one became Gum 40.

Much earlier, in 1888, Danish astronomer John Louis Emil Dreyer compiled the ambitious New General Catalogue, or NGC, listing 7840 objects. He later added two Index Catalogues with 5386 more, and there this nebula is IC 2872. Because better telescopes keep finding new objects, such catalogues will never be complete.
explore: The New General Catalogue is still in use today, and it received its latest update in 2019. An emission nebula is a cloud of gas that glows because energetic light from nearby stars excites it.

caption: A laser guide star beneath the Large Magellanic Cloud, Paranal Observatory, Chile
story: Yepun, one of the four 8.2-metre Unit Telescopes of ESO's Very Large Telescope, fires a laser beam into the dark sky over Paranal Observatory in this photograph by ESO Photo Ambassador Petr Horálek. Above it hangs the Large Magellanic Cloud, a barred spiral galaxy in orbit around our own. A faint white glow marks its older stars, while iridescent magenta and blue show its young stellar nurseries.

The laser creates an artificial star, a Laser Guide Star, which helps astronomers cope with Earth's atmosphere. The air blurs and distorts starlight, so astronomers place the laser star near the patch of sky they are observing and measure the tiny flickers in its image.

The VLT's adaptive optics system uses that reference to correct for the shifting atmosphere, producing the sharpest possible images in the main observations. The Large Magellanic Cloud, like the Small Magellanic Cloud, has been studied many times by ESO telescopes.
explore: Because the Magellanic Clouds are so close, their nebulae and star clusters can be seen in detail, making them rewarding targets for amateur and professional astronomers alike.
